title: CFA Economics: Supply, demand and elasticity
subtitle: Why raising prices sometimes lifts revenue and sometimes kills it
openingQuestion: An airline raises fares 10% and revenue falls 15%. Is demand for this product elastic or inelastic?
openingOptions: Inelastic, because passengers still have to fly whatever the fare
Elastic: quantity demanded falls by more than the price rise
Unit elastic, since both price and quantity have changed
Impossible to say without knowing the airline's cost base
explanation: Price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. Revenue falling when price rises means quantity fell by more than 10%, so the absolute value of the coefficient is greater than 1 - demand is elastic. The rule to remember: with elastic demand, price and revenue move in opposite directions; with inelastic demand, they move together.

realWorldExample.company: Domestic air fares at Tet versus an ordinary week
realWorldExample.description: On an ordinary week passengers can easily shift their dates or take a coach, so demand is elastic - the airline discounts to fill seats. At Tet, the trip home is close to obligatory and there is no substitute available in time, so demand turns inelastic - the airline raises fares sharply, loses very few passengers and still grows revenue. The same product, with elasticity changing according to context.

quiz.question: Which factor makes demand for a product MORE elastic with respect to price?
options: It is a staple that consumers have to buy no matter the price
It has many substitutes and takes a large share of spending
There are few suppliers, so prices are easily pushed up
It is state-subsidised, so the price has been stable
quiz.explanation: Three factors mainly make demand more elastic: (1) plenty of substitutes, so the buyer can easily go elsewhere; (2) the item takes a large share of the budget, so the buyer pays close attention to price; (3) a longer time frame, since more time means more ways to substitute. A staple with no substitute, and a purchase of small value, run the other way and are inelastic. Concentration among suppliers affects the price level rather than the buyer's sensitivity to it.

quiz.question: What does a negative income elasticity of demand mean?
options: A necessity: the quantity bought barely moves with income
A luxury good: a rise in income means buying considerably more
An inferior good: a rise in income means buying less of it
A complement: it has to be bought alongside another product
quiz.explanation: Negative income elasticity is the definition of an inferior good - income rises and quantity demanded falls. The classic examples are instant noodles and bus travel: as income rises, consumers switch to fresh food and private transport. Positive income elasticity above 1 marks a luxury; between 0 and 1 marks a necessity; and complementarity is measured by cross elasticity, not by income elasticity at all.

quiz.question: Cross elasticity between coffee and tea is positive. What does that tell you?
options: Both products are inferior goods in that market
The two products are complements bought together
The two products are completely unrelated goods
The two products are substitutes for each other
quiz.explanation: Positive cross elasticity means a rise in the price of A raises the quantity demanded of B - the signature of substitutes. Negative cross elasticity indicates complements (a printer and its ink: if printers get dearer, demand for ink falls). Cross elasticity near zero means the two products are unrelated. Whether either good is inferior is a separate question, answered by income elasticity rather than by the cross measure.

quiz.question: Demand for a product has a price elasticity of −0.3. If the company raises price 10%, what happens to revenue?
options: Up about 7%, because volume falls only 3% while price rises a full 10%
Down about 3%, because the volume lost outweighs the price gained per unit
Unchanged, because a price rise and a volume fall always cancel out
Down about 7%, since inelastic demand sends every buyer to substitutes
quiz.explanation: An absolute value below 1 means demand is inelastic: quantity responds less than price, so a price rise lifts revenue. Here 10% × 0.3 = 3% of volume lost against 10% of price gained, roughly +7%. The rule to remember: inelastic demand means price and revenue move together, elastic demand means they move in opposite directions.

quiz.question: Why is demand for a product usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run?
options: Because consumer incomes always rise gradually over time
Because buyers have time to find substitutes and change habits
Because long-run inflation lowers that item's relative price
Because the number of firms selling the item always falls over time
quiz.explanation: Petrol goes up and you still fill the tank this week, but a few years later people buy a more efficient car, switch to public transport, or move closer to work. That adjustment period is what makes long-run demand more elastic - and what makes a revenue forecast built on a short-run coefficient go wrong. Incomes rising, and inflation eroding relative prices, shift the demand curve rather than changing its slope.

keyTakeaways: Elasticity = % change in quantity / % change in price; an absolute value above 1 is elastic, below 1 inelastic
Elastic demand: a price rise LOWERS revenue. Inelastic demand: a price rise RAISES revenue
Demand is more elastic where there are many substitutes, where the item takes a large share of spending, and over longer horizons
Negative income elasticity = an inferior good; positive cross elasticity = substitutes, negative = complements

practicePrompt.question: A coffee chain wants to raise prices 8%. Analysis estimates the price elasticity of demand at −0.6. What happens to revenue, and why?
options: Revenue falls about 8%, because a price rise always drives buyers away
Revenue rises about 3.2%: demand falls only 4.8%, less than the 8% price rise
Revenue is unchanged, because price and volume effects always cancel out
It cannot be estimated without knowing the chain's gross profit margin
practicePrompt.explanation: With a coefficient of −0.6 (inelastic), an 8% price rise cuts quantity demanded by roughly 8% × 0.6 = 4.8%. Revenue changes by approximately +8% − 4.8% ≈ +3.2%. This is why brands with a loyal customer base (inelastic demand) have pricing power - but note that the estimate only holds for small price changes, and says nothing about profit if costs move as well.

summary.keyIdea: Elasticity measures how sensitive quantity demanded is to price, to income or to the price of another good - and it decides whether a price rise lifts revenue or sinks it.
summary.commonMistake: Assuming a price rise always lifts revenue, or always lowers it - the answer depends entirely on elasticity
summary.action: Before any pricing decision, estimate the elasticity of demand rather than guessing at it

application.title: Applying this in CFA analysis
application.message: Elasticity is the foundational tool for assessing a company's pricing power - a factor that feeds directly into sustainable margins when you build a valuation model.
application.secondary: In Equity Investments, businesses facing inelastic demand usually command a higher multiple, because they can pass rising input costs on to customers when inflation picks up.

sections.text: Supply and demand are the foundation of economics, but the part that is genuinely usable in financial analysis is elasticity: the number that tells you whether a business has pricing power.
Supply, demand and the equilibrium point

The demand curve slopes down: the higher the price, the fewer the buyers. The supply curve slopes up: the higher the price, the more producers want to sell. Where the two cross is the equilibrium price and quantity. One distinction matters: MOVING ALONG the demand curve is caused by a change in price, whereas SHIFTING the whole curve is caused by something else changing (income, tastes, the price of related goods, expectations). Confusing the two is the single most common error in exam questions.
The three elasticities to know cold

items: Price elasticity: % change in quantity demanded / % change in price. Decides whether a price rise lifts or lowers revenue
Income elasticity: positive and above 1 is a luxury, positive and below 1 is a necessity, negative is an inferior good
Cross elasticity: positive means substitutes, negative means complements, near zero means unrelated

sections.text: Elasticity translates directly into pricing power. A business facing inelastic demand - a strong brand, few substitutes, customers locked into an ecosystem - can raise prices with inflation without losing customers, so its margins hold up better through the cycle. This is why the market pays different valuation multiples to two companies growing revenue at the same rate.

sections.label: A note for the CFA exam
sections.text: Exam questions often turn on sign and magnitude: price elasticity is almost always negative (price up, quantity down), so it is usually discussed in absolute value. When a question says 'elasticity of 0.6' without a sign, read it as the absolute value - that is, inelastic.

diagram.label: Supply and demand meet at the equilibrium point
Measure elasticity: to price, to income, to the price of related goods
Inelastic demand → a price rise lifts revenue
Elastic demand → a price rise lowers revenue
From there, infer the firm's pricing power
